p.src: The tale tells how Vice Minister Dongxian, seeing that Tanzhou had fallen, had no choice but to flee the city, escorted by Yao'er Weikang. They ran straight into Lin Chong and Guan Sheng, and a fierce battle ensued; but how could they have any heart to prolong the fight? They veered off diagonally and fought their way out for dear life. Guan Sheng and Lin Chong were intent on seizing the city and did not pursue them, but instead rushed inside.

p.src: Meanwhile, Song Jiang led the main host into Tanzhou and scattered the Liao troops. He issued proclamations to reassure soldiers and civilians alike, forbidding the slightest offense against them, and ordered every warship to be brought into the city. At the same time he rewarded the whole army. Of the Liao officials serving in the city, those of Chinese surname were retained in their former posts, while all the tribal officials without Chinese surnames were expelled from the city and sent back to the desert. He also wrote a memorial reporting to the court that Tanzhou had been taken. All the money, silks, gold, and treasure in the government storehouses were escorted to the capital. He wrote as well to Grand Commandant Su, asking him to memorialize the matter. When the Son of Heaven heard the report, he was greatly delighted. He immediately issued an edict appointing Zhao, Assistant Prefect of the Eastern Capital, as imperial pacification commissioner, and sent him with twenty thousand soldiers of the Imperial Camp to supervise the campaign.

p.src: When word of this reached Song Jiang and the others, they led the commanders far beyond the city walls to welcome him, then escorted him into the prefectural offices at Tanzhou, where he lodged and provisionally established his field headquarters. All the commanders and leaders came to pay their respects, and the formal greetings were completed. This Commissioner Zhao was in fact a scion of the imperial Zhao clan. He was generous, humane, and virtuous, and upright in all his dealings. Grand Commandant Su had recommended him before the emperor, who had therefore specially sent him to the frontier to supervise the troops. Commissioner Zhao was greatly pleased when he witnessed Song Jiang's benevolence and virtue. He said, “His Majesty already knows how devotedly all you commanders have served and how sorely the soldiers have labored. He has specially sent me to supervise the army at the front, bringing twenty-five cartloads of gold, silver, and silks as rewards. Whenever anyone renders extraordinary service, I shall report it to the court and request an official rank and title for him. Now that you, General, have taken this prefecture, I shall make a further report to the court. All you commanders must give your utmost loyalty and strength, swiftly accomplish this great work, and return victorious to the capital; the emperor will assuredly entrust you with high office.” Song Jiang and the others bowed their thanks and said, “May we trouble Your Excellency the Commissioner to hold Tanzhou while we divide our forces and seize the vital prefectures of Liao, leaving the enemy unable to aid either head or tail.” They distributed the imperial rewards among the officers and men, recalled the armies from every route to await new orders, and prepared to seize the prefectures of Liao. Yang Xiong reported, “Jizhou lies close ahead. It is a great prefecture, rich in money and provisions and abundant in rice and wheat—the treasury of Liao. Once Jizhou is taken, all the other places may be seized.” After hearing him out, Song Jiang summoned the strategist Wu Yong to confer.

p.src: Meanwhile, as Vice Minister Dongxian and Yao'er Weikang were heading east, they encountered Chu Mingyu and Cao Mingji leading a remnant of defeated troops, and together they fled to Jizhou. Entering the city, they went before Prince Yelü Dezhong, the emperor's brother, and reported, “Song Jiang's army is immense. Among his men is a southern barbarian who uses stones and is extraordinarily formidable. His stones strike the mark every time, never once missing, and he is deadly at felling men. Both imperial nephews and the young general Aliqi were all killed by his stones.” Prince Yelü said, “If that is so, remain here and help me kill that barbarian.” Before he had finished speaking, a swift scout galloped in with a report: “Song Jiang has divided his army into two columns to attack Jizhou. One has reached Pingyu County, and the other Yutian County.” On hearing this, the imperial prince immediately ordered Vice Minister Dongxian, “Lead your own troops and hold the pass at Pingyu County, but do not engage them. I shall first lead my troops to capture the barbarians at Yutian County, then sweep around behind those at Pingyu County. Where will they have left to flee? Meanwhile, send urgent word to Bazhou and Youzhou, ordering the armies on those two routes to come to our aid.” Jizhou had in fact been entrusted by the ruler of Liao to his younger brother Yelü Dezhong, who commanded four sons: his eldest, Zongyun, and his second, Zongdian; his third, Zonglei, and his fourth, Zonglin. Under him were more than ten battle commanders, including a commander-in-chief named Baomisheng and a deputy commander named Tianshanyong, who guarded the city of Jizhou. At once the imperial prince instructed Baomisheng to defend the city, while he personally led the main army, taking his four sons and the deputy commander Tianshanyong, and sped toward Yutian County.

Lu Junyi, meanwhile, led numerous battle commanders and thirty thousand troops to Yutian County, where they soon drew close to the Liao army. What plan can bring us victory?” Zhu Wu replied, “In my humble opinion, since we do not know their terrain, the armies must not advance rashly. We should array our columns in the form of a long serpent, head and tail supporting one another in an unbroken circuit. p.src: Yellow sands stretched boundlessly; black mists billowed thick. Black-eagle banners unfurled like a bank of dark clouds; flanking cavalry churned up a murderous aura that filled half the sky. Their green felt hats resembled lotus leaves across a thousand ponds, stirring in a gentle breeze; Their iron helmets were like a boundless ocean frozen beneath the sun. Every man wore his robe fastened to the left, and every man's hair hung level with his shoulders. They were heavily clad in linked iron armor and tightly bound in stitched battle robes. The hardy frontier soldiers had dark faces, blue eyes, and yellow beards; Their Tatar horses roared, broad of shoulder, steel of loin, and iron of hoof. Horn bows clustered with tamarisk arrows; tiger-skin robes pressed against narrow carved saddles. Born on the frontier, they grew up able to draw the strongest bows; Their people native to the northern lands, they were reared to ride the wildest horses. Bronze barbarian drums beat before the army, while reed-leaf pipes sounded from horseback.

p.src: Prince Yelü Dezhong, the emperor's brother, had led his troops to Yutian County first and drawn them up in battle formation. In the Song army, Zhu Wu climbed a cloud ladder to inspect it, then descended and reported to Vanguard Commander Lu, “The formation laid out by the Liao men is the Five Tigers Leaning on the Mountain Formation. There is nothing remarkable about it.” Zhu Wu then mounted the command platform, waved the signal flags leftward and wheeled them rightward, directing the troops until he too had formed an array. Lu Junyi looked at it but did not recognize it, and asked, “What formation is this?” Zhu Wu said, “This is the Kun Transforming into a Peng Formation.” Lu Junyi asked, “What is meant by ‘the kun transforming into a peng’?” Zhu Wu replied, “In the Northern Sea there is a fish named the kun, which can transform into the great peng and fly ninety thousand li in a single ascent. Viewed from afar or close at hand, this formation seems no more than a small array; but when the enemy comes to attack, it transforms into a great one. That is why it is called ‘the kun transforming into a peng.’” Lu Junyi heard this and praised him without cease.

p.src: In the center stood the Prince Imperial, with four young generals, two on either side. From each of their shoulders hung a small bright mirror, edged with black tassels. Four fine sabers and four swift horses stood arrayed in perfect order before the battle line. Behind the Prince Imperial, rank upon rank, stood a great many other fighting generals. The four young generals shouted, “You wretched bandits! How dare you violate our frontier!” Hearing this, Lu Junyi asked, “With the two armies facing one another, which hero will ride out first?” Before he had finished, Guan Sheng the Great Blade brandished his Green Dragon Crescent Blade and spurred out ahead of the rest. From the other side, the foreign general Yelü Zongyun flourished his saber and galloped forth to meet Guan Sheng. Before they had exchanged five bouts, Yelü Zonglin brandished his saber, spurred forward, and came to assist. Seeing this, Huyan Zhuo raised his twin clubs and charged straight out to engage him. The brothers Yelü Zongdian and Yelü Zonglei leveled their sabers, leapt their horses forward, and joined the battle together. On this side, Xu Ning and Suo Chao each raised his weapon and rode out to meet them. The four pairs fought before the lines, tangled together in one seething mass.

p.src: While the fighting raged, Zhang Qing the Featherless Arrow saw his chance and quietly urged his horse toward the front. Some soldiers who had survived the defeat at Tanzhou recognized Zhang Qing and hurriedly reported to the Prince Imperial, “That savage in the green battle robe across from us is the man skilled at hurling stones. Now that he is urging his horse out, he means to use the same trick as before.” Tianshan Yong heard this and said, “Rest easy, Your Highness. I shall make that savage taste one of my crossbow bolts!” Tianshan Yong was an expert at using a lacquered crossbow from horseback. Its iron-fletched bolts, over a foot long, were famously called “Drops of Oil.” From the saddle, Tianshan Yong secured the weapon by its ring, then urged his horse out, letting two lieutenants screen him in front. The three riders quietly pressed straight toward the battle line. Zhang Qing spotted them first, slipped a stone into his hand, aimed at the leading foreign officer, and hurled it with a shout: “Take that!” The stone merely grazed the man’s helmet. But Tianshan Yong had slipped behind the other officer’s horse. With his bolt firmly set and string properly drawn, he waited until Zhang Qing was close, took aim, and shot straight at him. “Aiya!” cried Zhang Qing. He tried to dodge, but the bolt struck his throat, and he tumbled from his horse. Dong Ping the Double-Speared General and Shi Jin the Nine-Dragoned, leading Xie Zhen and Xie Bao, fought desperately forward and rescued him. When Vanguard Lu saw him, he quickly ordered the bolt pulled out. The blood would not stop flowing, so they immediately bound and supported his neck. He then ordered Zou Yuan and Zou Run to help Zhang Qing into a cart and escort him back to Tanzhou, where An Daoquan the Divine Physician was to treat him.

p.src: The cart had only just departed when shouts rose again at the front, and a report came: “A force is racing in from the northwest! Without exchanging a word, they are charging headlong and have broken into our formation!” Seeing Zhang Qing felled by a bolt, Lu Junyi had no heart to continue the battle. His four generals each feigned defeat and withdrew. The four foreign generals pursued their advantage; the foreign troops from the northwest swept in obliquely; and the main foreign host opposite them surged forward like a collapsing mountain. How could they reform their battle array there? The officers and men were cut into scattered fragments, unable to aid one another. Lu Junyi alone, with one horse and one spear, fought his way through to the far side. Toward evening, the four young generals happened to return and came face-to-face with Lu Junyi. Alone with a single horse and spear, he held off all four foreign generals without the least sign of fear. After they had fought for about two hours, Lu Junyi seized his chance and offered an opening. Yelü Zonglin slashed into it, but Lu Junyi gave a mighty shout. Caught unprepared, the foreign general took a spear thrust and was knocked from his horse. The other three young generals were startled and showed fear. Losing the will to fight, they spurred away. Lu Junyi dismounted, drew his saber, cut off Yelü Zonglin’s head, and tied it beneath his horse’s neck. He remounted and headed south. Encountering another band of some thousand Liao troops, he charged into them and scattered them in every direction. Before he had gone another few li, he encountered yet another body of troops.

p.src: The moonless night made it impossible to tell whose troops they were, but their voices proved to be those of men of Song. Lu Junyi called, “Who are the approaching troops?” Huyan Zhuo answered. Overjoyed, Lu Junyi joined forces with him. Huyan Zhuo said, “The Liao troops scattered us, and we could not come to one another’s aid. I broke through their formation and fought my way here with Han Tao and Peng Qi. I do not know what became of the other generals.” Lu Junyi replied, “I fought four generals at once, killed one of them, and drove the other three away. Afterward I ran into more than a thousand men and scattered them as well. On reaching this place, I never expected to meet you, General.” The two rode side by side, leading their followers southward. After scarcely a dozen li, they found troops blocking the road ahead. Huyan Zhuo called, “How can we fight in this darkness? Let us decide life or death at daybreak!” Someone across from them heard and asked, “Can the newcomer be General Huyan Zhuo?” Recognizing the voice as that of Guan Sheng the Great Blade, Huyan Zhuo called back, “Chief Lu is here!” All the chiefs dismounted and sat down together on the grass. Lu Junyi and Huyan Zhuo recounted what had happened to them. Guan Sheng said, “When the battle went against us, we were unable to aid one another. Xuan Zan, Hao Siwen, Shan Tinggui, Wei Dingguo, and I sought an escape route on our five horses. Later we gathered over a thousand soldiers and came here. Knowing nothing of the terrain, we lay in wait beside the road here, intending to move on at daybreak. We never expected to encounter you, elder brother.” They united their forces.

p.src: They waited out the night until dawn, then gradually made their way south again. As they neared Yutian County, they saw a body of troops scouting the road. On looking closely, they found Dong Ping the Double-Speared General, Xu Ning the Golden-Lance Bearer, and their comrades. They had all taken up quarters in Yutian County and driven off the Liao troops. p.src: The two sides drew up their battle lines, and the Liao general Baomisheng rode forth with his spear held crosswise. Seeing him before the lines, Song Jiang called out, “To slay the enemy general and seize his banner—that shall win the highest merit!” Before he had finished speaking, Lin Chong, the “Panther Head,” charged out from the ranks and engaged the Liao general Baomisheng in fierce combat. They fought for more than thirty bouts without either gaining the upper hand. Eager to claim the foremost merit, Lin Chong wielded his eighteen-foot serpent spear. When the struggle was at its fiercest, he gave a thunderous roar, swept aside his opponent’s long spear, and thrust the serpent spear into Baomisheng’s neck, knocking him from his horse. Song Jiang was overjoyed. Both armies raised a tremendous shout. When the Liao general Tianshanyong saw Baomisheng run through, he charged out with his spear held crosswise. From Song Jiang’s ranks, Xu Ning leveled his hooked spear and rode straight to meet him. Their horses met, but before they had fought twenty bouts, Xu Ning raised his spear and thrust Tianshanyong from the saddle. Delighted to see two enemy generals defeated in succession, Song Jiang ordered his troops into a general melee. The Liao army was routed and fled toward Jizhou. Song Jiang’s forces pursued them for more than ten li before withdrawing and returning.

p.src: That day Song Jiang pitched camp and rewarded the officers and men of the three armies. The next day he issued orders to strike camp, and the whole army advanced straight upon Jizhou. On the third day, the Prince Imperial was greatly alarmed at the loss of two generals; then another report came: “The Song army has arrived!” He hurriedly said to Chamberlain Dongxian, “Lead this force out of the city to meet the enemy and help relieve me of this burden.” Chamberlain Dongxian dared not disobey. Taking Yao'er Weikang, Chu Mingyu, and Cao Mingji with him, he led a thousand troops out and arrayed them beneath the city walls. As Song Jiang’s army neared the city, it spread out like the wings of a wild goose. The standard at the gate opened aside, and Suo Chao rode before the lines with his great axe resting crosswise. From the Liao ranks, Yao'er Weikang immediately rushed out to meet him. Without exchanging a word, the two generals clashed and fought for more than twenty bouts. In the end the Liao general lost his nerve; with no heart to continue the fight, he could only turn to flee. Suo Chao spurred after him, swung the great axe aloft with both hands, took aim at the Liao general’s crown, and brought it crashing down, cleaving Yao'er Weikang’s head in two. At this sight, Chamberlain Dongxian hastily ordered Chu Mingyu and Cao Mingji to go to his aid. Those two were already thoroughly frightened, but, pressed beyond refusal, they had no choice but to level their spears and advance from the lines. When Shi Jin, the “Nine-Dragoned,” saw two generals emerge together from the Liao army, he brandished his saber, urged on his horse, and charged straight at them. Displaying all his heroic prowess, Shi Jin raised his saber and brought it down, first cutting Chu Mingyu from his horse. Cao Mingji made haste to flee, but Shi Jin overtook him and likewise cut him from the saddle with a single blow. Shi Jin spurred his horse into the Liao formation. Seeing this, Song Jiang pointed with the tip of his whip and drove his troops forward in force, slaughtering their way to the drawbridge. When Yelü Dezhong saw this, his distress deepened. He ordered the city gates tightly secured and all his generals onto the walls to defend them vigilantly; at the same time, he sent a memorial to the sovereign and dispatched men to Bazhou and Youzhou to seek reinforcements.

p.src: Now Shi Qian was a man who could fly over eaves and run along walls; to him, scaling walls and crossing fortifications was as easy as walking on level ground. He first went up the pagoda at Baoyan Temple and kindled a fire there. The pagoda was the highest structure around, and when the blaze rose, everyone inside and outside the city could see it. Its light shone for more than thirty li around, like a fiery awl boring into the sky. He then returned and set fire to the Buddha hall. With those two fires blazing, the whole city erupted into turmoil. In every household, old and young were thrown into panic; sons wailed and daughters wept as people of all ages fled for their lives. Shi Xiu climbed straight onto the roof of the Jizhou government offices and started a fire beneath the bargeboard. When the people of Jizhou saw fires rising in three places, they knew spies were at work. They had no heart left to defend the walls and could no longer be restrained; each fled home to protect his own household. Before long another fire broke out inside the temple gate: after leaving Baoyan Temple, Shi Qian had set yet one more blaze. The Prince Imperial saw that there was not a moment’s peace anywhere in the city and that fires were raging along four or five routes. He realized Song Jiang had men inside the walls. In frantic haste, he gathered his forces, took his family and his two children, loaded them into carts, opened the northern gate, and fled. Seeing the troops inside the city fall into disorder, Song Jiang urged his soldiers to sweep forward and fight their way in. Battle cries shook heaven both inside and outside the walls, and the southern gate was soon taken. Chamberlain Dongxian, seeing that their few could not withstand the enemy’s many, had no choice but to follow the Prince Imperial and flee through the northern gate.

p.src: Song Jiang led the main body of his army into Jizhou and immediately issued orders that the wind-driven fires on every side be extinguished first. At daybreak, proclamations were posted to reassure the people of Jizhou. He brought all the troops into Jizhou to be quartered there, and rewarded the officers and men of the three armies. In the register of merit, the achievements and ranking of Shi Xiu and Shi Qian were prominently recorded. He then sent an official dispatch informing Pacification Commissioner Zhao that the great prefecture of Jizhou had been captured, and inviting His Excellency to come and take up his quarters there. Pacification Commissioner Zhao sent a written reply: “For the time being I shall remain encamped at Tanzhou. Vanguard Commander Song is to hold Jizhou securely. The summer heat is now upon us and the weather is oppressive; this is no time to move the army. When the weather grows a little cooler, we shall consider our next move.” Upon receiving the reply, Song Jiang ordered Lu Junyi to take command of the officers and troops originally assigned to him and encamp at Yutian County, while the rest of the main army remained to hold Jizhou. They were to await cooler weather and further orders.

p.src: Now Prince Yelü Dezhong, the emperor’s brother, and Chamberlain Dongxian took their families with them and fled back to Youzhou, then went straight on to Yanjing to appear before the sovereign of Liao. Meanwhile, the sovereign of Liao ascended his throne in the Golden Hall, where the civil and military officials of both ranks assembled and completed their morning audience. The Chief Commissioner of the Palace Gate reported, “Your Majesty’s brother, the Prince of Jizhou, has returned and is waiting at the gate.” On hearing the report, the sovereign hurriedly ordered him summoned, and he was ushered below the throne. Yelü Dezhong and Chamberlain Dongxian prostrated themselves below the imperial steps and burst into loud weeping. The sovereign said, “My beloved brother, cease your grieving for the moment. Whatever has happened, tell me everything without reserve.” Yelü Dezhong reported, “The boy emperor of Song dispatched Song Jiang at the head of an army to campaign against us. His forces are so powerful that we cannot withstand them. They have cost me my two sons and slain four of our great commanders at Tanzhou. The Song army swept onward and Jizhou, too, fell into their hands. I have come before Your Majesty to beg for death!” When the sovereign of Great Liao heard this, he issued an imperial command: “Rise for now. We shall deliberate carefully here.” The sovereign asked, “Who is this southern barbarian leading the troops? How can he have such formidable followers?” Grand Preceptor Chu Jian, Right Chancellor among the assembled officials, stepped from the ranks and reported, “I have heard that Song Jiang and his band were originally outlaws from the stronghold in the marshes of Liangshan, yet they refused to harm innocent people. They devoted themselves to carrying out Heaven’s justice, killing only corrupt and lawless officials and those who deceived and oppressed the common people. Later, Tong Guan and Gao Qiu led armies to capture them, but in only five engagements Song Jiang slaughtered their forces so thoroughly that not a scrap of armor returned. Those heroes could not be suppressed or captured. The boy emperor sent envoys three times with edicts offering them amnesty. At last they all submitted, but Song Jiang was merely made a vanguard commander without receiving a substantive official appointment, while all the others remained commoners. Now the emperor has sent them here to fight us. They claim that their company numbers one hundred and eight, corresponding to the stars of Heaven. These men are extraordinarily formidable. Your Majesty must not underestimate them!” The sovereign said, “If what you say is true, then what are we to do?” An official emerged from the clustered ranks. It was Chamberlain Ouyang, his ceremonial robe trailing on the floor and an ivory tablet held before his breast. He memorialized, “Long life to Your Majesty! Though I possess little ability, I would offer a modest stratagem that can drive back the Song army.” The sovereign was delighted. “Since you have sound counsel, speak at once.” Chamberlain Ouyang spoke at length; before a single audience had ended, his words were destined to make Song Jiang’s name illustrious in history and his deeds recorded in the vermilion annals. Indeed, the scheme devised to defend the realm would outwit Lü Wang, and the achievement accomplished in accord with Heaven would rival Zhang Liang. But what proposal did Chamberlain Ouyang make? Listen to the explanation in the next chapter.
